task_row_model.query: For an adult patient with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, what is the recommended first-line antibiotic and usual treatment duration, and what antibiotic should be used if the patient has an immediate-type penicillin allergy in a region where macrolide resistance exceeds 25%?

documents.content: Clinical Practice Guideline — Adult Acute Bacterial Rhinosinusitis. For uncomplicated adult cases the guideline endorses oral amoxicillin–clavulanate as first-line therapy. Typical outpatient duration for otherwise healthy adults is 5–7 days; therapy may be extended to 10–14 days for patients with severe symptoms, slow response, or comorbidities. The guideline summarizes diagnostic criteria and provides dosing ranges but emphasizes the initial choice of amoxicillin–clavulanate over macrolides in most patients. Background sections define rhinosinusitis and review common causative pathogens; those definitional passages are included for completeness but do not change the primary antibiotic recommendation.
documents.reasoning_trace: Contains the primary recommendation (oral amoxicillin–clavulanate) and the stated treatment durations (5–7 days, extend 10–14 days for severe/comorbid).

documents.content: Allergy and Alternative Therapy Note (clinic memo). When patients report an immediate-type (IgE-mediated) penicillin allergy, clinicians should avoid beta-lactams. The memo recommends doxycycline as the preferred non–beta-lactam alternative in adults for community sinus infections; it warns that macrolides are unreliable where macrolide resistance is high. A brief case vignette contrasts doxycycline response versus macrolide failure in an area with elevated macrolide resistance. The note uses plain clinical language and practical prescribing advice rather than formal guideline formatting.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides alternative for immediate-type penicillin allergy (doxycycline) and cautions against macrolide use where macrolide resistance is high.

documents.content: Health News Brief — Rising Macrolide Resistance. Surveillance reports in several regions now show macrolide resistance rates in common upper respiratory pathogens exceeding 25%, prompting experts to advise against empirical macrolide use for community sinus infections in those areas. Journalists cite infectious-disease consultants who recommend doxycycline as the preferred alternative to penicillin-class drugs when allergy is present. The piece includes commentary about stewardship and resistance trends, and it notes that azithromycin failures have been reported in high-resistance locales.
documents.reasoning_trace: Documents the threshold (>25%) for avoiding macrolides and supports doxycycline as the preferred alternative in the context of penicillin allergy.

documents.content: Historical Review: Sulfonamides and Early Antimicrobials. Before widespread availability of penicillins, sulfonamides were the mainstay for many upper respiratory infections; case reports from the 1940s described varying efficacy. This narrative review traces the evolution of antibiotic classes, surgical drainage techniques, and shifts in outpatient prescribing habits. Several unrelated case studies from mid-20th-century hospitals are summarized to illustrate historical practice, but the review does not provide current therapeutic recommendations or resistance thresholds relevant to contemporary clinical decision-making.
documents.reasoning_trace: Noise: historical context and unrelated case studies; no current treatment recommendations used.

documents.content: Epidemiology Report Excerpt. Ambulatory care data show that acute sinusitis accounts for a substantial proportion of primary care visits; one table lists annual visit counts and age distribution. The report also presents regional outpatient antibiotic prescribing rates and notes variability between urban and rural settings. Although the dataset includes some antibiotic classes among prescriptions, it primarily focuses on visit frequency and demographic patterns rather than specific guideline-based agent selection or allergy management.
documents.reasoning_trace: Noise: provides epidemiologic and prescribing-rate context but no specific guideline recommendations for first-line therapy or allergy alternatives.

task_row_model.golden_answer: For adult acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, oral amoxicillin–clavulanate is recommended first-line; uncomplicated cases are treated for 5–7 days (extend to 10–14 days for severe disease or comorbidity). In patients with immediate-type penicillin allergy, doxycycline is the preferred alternative; macrolides should be avoided when local macrolide resistance exceeds 25%.
